summary: Describes authentication methods and security mechanisms for LDAP. It covers using StartTLS to set up TLS, simple bind (anonymous, unauthenticated and name/password), SASL bind including EXTERNAL, and the authentication and authorization states of a session. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4513 explains how an LDAP client proves an identity and how the client and server protect information sent between them. It also clarifies that an empty password does not authenticate a named user.

subtitle: How LDAP checks identity and protects a session with StartTLS, simple Bind or SASL.

tldr.problem: LDAP clients and servers need interoperable ways to authenticate users and protect directory data from observers or attackers on the network path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines StartTLS, three simple Bind mechanisms, SASL Bind, and the authorization states a server assigns to a session.
tldr.outcome: It establishes a common minimum set of LDAP security functions. RFC 4513 obsoletes RFC 2251, RFC 2829 and RFC 2830, and is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4513 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2251, RFC 2829 and RFC 2830. It has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Threats and LDAP Security Tools
sections.content:
LDAP lets clients search, retrieve and change directory information. The RFC lists risks from hostile clients and from attackers on the path, including unauthorized reading or changes, stolen credentials, denial of service, spoofing and session hijacking.

LDAP uses Bind for authentication and can use TLS or SASL for data integrity and confidentiality. Servers can also set resource limits and use local access-control systems, but LDAP does not define a standard access-control facility. The RFC sets common implementation requirements so clients and servers can interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory data can be read or changed by the wrong party, and passwords can be exposed while they travel. LDAP uses authentication and connection protection to reduce these risks.

sections.title: Minimum Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
Every LDAP server MUST support anonymous authentication using simple Bind. An implementation that supports another authentication method MUST also support name/password simple Bind and be able to protect it with TLS established through StartTLS. Implementations SHOULD disable name/password authentication by default when suitable data protection is absent.

Servers SHOULD support the SASL EXTERNAL mechanism. Implementations that support TLS MUST support TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA and SHOULD support TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, as specified by this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: All servers must allow an anonymous session. A server that accepts password authentication must also support protecting that password with TLS.

sections.title: Starting TLS and Checking the Server
sections.content:
StartTLS establishes TLS within an existing LDAP session. A client MUST check the server identity in its certificate to prevent a man-in-the-middle attack. The normal check compares the name or address used by the client with matching subjectAltName values. A DNS wildcard may appear only as the leftmost label and matches one label.

If the client will use both Bind and StartTLS, it SHOULD establish TLS first so the Bind exchange is protected. After TLS starts, the client SHOULD discard or refresh server capability information obtained through insecure means. Both sides decide whether the negotiated security level meets their local policy; StartTLS alone does not provide security apart from the TLS layer.
sections.plainLanguage: StartTLS adds TLS protection to the LDAP session. Before relying on it, the client checks that the certificate identifies the server it intended to contact.

sections.title: The Session's Authorization State
sections.content:
An LDAP session has an authorization state that reflects its authentication and the security services in place. Authorization rules are local to the server. A client may send requests before binding; the server treats those requests as if an anonymous Bind had occurred.

When a Bind request arrives, the server first moves the session to an anonymous state. A successful Bind moves it to the requested state. A failed Bind leaves it anonymous. Starting, changing or closing a security layer can also affect the session state.
sections.plainLanguage: A new LDAP session starts without an authenticated identity. A successful Bind can establish one, while a failed Bind leaves the session anonymous.

sections.title: Three Simple Bind Mechanisms
sections.content:
Simple Bind has three mechanisms. Anonymous Bind uses an empty name and empty password. Unauthenticated Bind uses a non-empty distinguished name and an empty password, but the session remains anonymous; the name is only for logging and must not be used for authorization. Name/password Bind uses a non-empty distinguished name and password and establishes an authenticated state if accepted.

An empty password can accidentally trigger unauthenticated Bind. Clients SHOULD require an explicit choice and reject an empty password in a name/password interface. Servers SHOULD reject unauthenticated Bind by default. Name/password Bind is unsuitable without confidentiality protection because it discloses the password to the server and can expose it in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: An empty name and password create an anonymous session. A name without a password is still anonymous, so only a valid name and password can authenticate a user.

sections.title: SASL Bind and Security Risks
sections.content:
SASL lets LDAP use different authentication mechanisms. The SASL service name is ldap. A SASL exchange can take several Bind requests: the server sends a challenge with saslBindInProgress, and the client replies using the same mechanism. These challenges and responses are binary data, not Base64 text.

The EXTERNAL mechanism uses credentials established by a lower layer, such as a TLS client certificate. It fails with inappropriateAuthentication if no such credentials exist. Without integrity and confidentiality protection, attackers can read or change LDAP traffic or alter the advertised SASL mechanisms. Clients should check the available mechanisms again after integrity protection is installed.
sections.plainLanguage: SASL allows different identity checks to share one LDAP exchange format. Some checks involve several challenge-and-response messages, and TLS can provide the certificate credentials used by EXTERNAL.
